sections.h: Luke: two parables on prayer
sections.b: Luke alone tells the parable of the widow who wears down an unjust judge, told so that the disciples would "pray at all times and not grow weary" (Luke 18:1–8), and the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, whose plea "God, be gracious to me, the sinner" is heard while the Pharisee's thanksgiving for his own virtues is not (Luke 18:9–14). The first argues from the lesser to the greater: if even a crooked judge gives justice, God will give it to his chosen who cry to him day and night. The second shows that the prayer God hears comes from humility, not from merit. The tax collector's words became the root of the Orthodox Jesus Prayer. Luke's end-time discourse closes the same way: "Stay alert all the time. Keep praying" (Luke 21:36).

common: The widow and the judge teaches that God is the opposite of the judge, not that persistent prayer wears God down.
uncommon: Some readers take the widow parable as a picture of a powerless woman shaming a corrupt court, with no figure for God at all.

sections.h: Luke 18–21: parables on the way to Jerusalem
sections.b: In the last stretch of Luke's journey and in the temple, Jesus tells the widow and the judge (Luke 18:1–8) and the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14), both found only in Luke; the ten minas (Luke 19:11–27), which shares a core with Matthew's talents but adds a nobleman who goes to receive a kingdom and is rejected by his citizens, a story Jesus' hearers would have connected with Archelaus' trip to Rome in 4 BC; the tenants of the vineyard, told "to the people" (Luke 20:9–19); and the fig tree, with "and every tree" added (Luke 21:29–31). Luke states the purpose of three of them in advance (Luke 18:1, 9; 19:11), something he rarely does.

common: Luke's minas and Matthew's talents are usually thought to be two versions of one parable.
uncommon: Some read the nobleman of the minas as a picture of a cruel earthly king, not of Christ.

sections.h: Luke: three widows in the last chapters
sections.b: Luke's last chapters before the passion are framed by widows. A widow demands justice until even an unjust judge gives it (Luke 18:1–8). Jesus warns against scribes who "eat up widows' houses" (Luke 20:47). A poor widow drops her last two lepta into the temple treasury, her whole living (Luke 21:1–4). The scene can be read as praise of her self-giving, or, coming right after the warning against those who exploit widows and right before the prophecy of the temple's destruction, as a lament over a system that took everything she had. Many read it both ways at once.

common: The widow's offering has long been read as the model of giving that costs the giver.
uncommon: Addison Wright read the widow's offering as Jesus' lament over exploitation, not his praise.

sections.h: Luke: the Pharisee at prayer, and the Pharisees' last appearance
sections.b: Luke's parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14) is aimed at people who trust in their own righteousness and despise others, not at Pharisees as such. The Pharisee's fasting and tithing were real devotion, and Jewish prayer did thank God for one's lot (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 28b); the fault is his contempt for the man behind him. The Pharisees' last appearance in Luke's Gospel is at the entry to Jerusalem, where some ask Jesus to quiet his disciples (Luke 19:39). They play no part in Luke's account of his arrest and death, and in Acts the Pharisee Gamaliel and others defend the apostles (Acts 5:34–39; 23:9). Some scribes, probably Pharisees, approve Jesus' answer to the Sadducees (Luke 20:39).

common: The Pharisee in the parable is a portrait of self-righteousness that can appear in any religious community.

sections.h: Luke 18:14: the tax collector "justified"
sections.b: Luke's parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector ends with the Gospels' clearest use of Paul's key verb: the tax collector "went down to his home justified" (dedikaiōmenos), "rather than the other" (Luke 18:14). His only prayer was a plea for atonement (hilasthēti, "be gracious, make atonement", Luke 18:13). The parable has been read as a picture of justification by faith apart from works (Luther and the Reformers), and as a picture of the humble contrition that grace produces (the Catholic tradition); the card on Luke 18 sets the churches' views side by side.

sections.h: Luke 18–19: the rich leader and Zacchaeus
sections.b: Luke places two rich men side by side. The rich leader (only Luke calls him a leader) is told, "Sell everything you have and share it out among the poor," and grows sad, "a very rich man" (Luke 18:18–23); Jesus says how hard it is for those with money to enter the kingdom, but "what is impossible from the human side is possible with God" (Luke 18:27). In the next scene, at Jericho, the rich chief tax collector Zacchaeus gives half his possessions to the poor and repays fourfold anyone he cheated, and Jesus says, "Today salvation has come to this household" (Luke 19:8–9). Between them Luke shows what he means by the impossible made possible, and that salvation is visible in what a person does with money.

common: Zacchaeus is Luke's example of how a rich man can be saved.
uncommon: Some scholars read Zacchaeus' present tenses as a defense of what he already did, not a new resolve.

sections.h: Jericho in Jesus' last journey
sections.b: Jesus' last stop before Jerusalem was Jericho, then a wealthy oasis of palms and balsam with Herodian palaces, on the pilgrim road from Perea. Near it he healed a blind beggar who called him Son of David (Luke 18:35–43; Mark 10:46–52, as he left; Matthew 20:29–34, two men). In the town he called the chief tax collector Zacchaeus down from a fig tree and stayed at his house (Luke 19:1–10), and there he told the parable of the nobleman who went away to receive a kingdom (Luke 19:11–27), a story that fits Archelaus, who rebuilt the Jericho palace. The road up to Jerusalem climbs about a kilometer through the wilderness of the good Samaritan's parable (Luke 10:30).

sections.h: Zacchaeus: repentance that pays back
sections.b: Zacchaeus' response to Jesus' visit is the New Testament's clearest picture of repentance in money: half his possessions to the poor, and fourfold to anyone he had cheated by false charges (Luke 19:8). The Law required the full amount plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7); fourfold was the penalty for stealing a sheep (Exodus 22:1; 2 Samuel 12:6). John the Baptist had told tax collectors to collect no more than their due (Luke 3:12–14). Jesus' verdict, "Today salvation has come to this household" and "the Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it" (Luke 19:9–10), sums up the parables of the lost in Luke 15.
sections.refs: Luke 19:1–10; Luke 3:12–14; Luke 15:1–32; Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7

sections.h: Luke's entry: a King, without palms
sections.b: Luke's account (Luke 19:28–40) has no branches and no "Hosanna"; the disciples spread cloaks and "set" Jesus on the colt, the verb used of Solomon's coronation (1 Kings 1:33). The acclaim comes from "the whole throng of disciples," not the city's crowds, and Luke alone adds "King" to Psalm 118:26 and "In heaven, peace! And glory in the highest!", an answer to the angels' song at the birth (Luke 2:14). Only Luke has the Pharisees' protest and Jesus' reply, "the stones will shout it out" (Luke 19:40; Habakkuk 2:11), and, as he comes near, his tears over the city (Luke 19:41–44).
sections.refs: Luke 19:28–44; Psalm 118:26; 1 Kings 1:33–40; Luke 2:14; Habakkuk 2:11; Mark 11:1–10

common: Luke's omission of branches and Hosannas is often explained as softening nationalist overtones for Gentile readers.

sections.h: Luke: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem
sections.b: Only Luke tells that Jesus wept aloud when he first saw the city, because it did not recognize "what leads to peace" or "the season when you were visited" (Luke 19:41–44). He foretells a siege: a palisade, encirclement, the city leveled with its children, not a stone left on a stone. Josephus describes Titus doing just this in AD 70 (War 5.491–511). In the discourse Luke adds "when you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps" and "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:20–24). The tone throughout is grief, like Jeremiah's.

common: Most scholars see in Luke 19:43–44 and 21:20–24 the siege of AD 70.
uncommon: C. H. Dodd argued that the language comes from the Old Testament's sieges, not from AD 70.

sections.h: Luke: the temple cleared, taught in, and doomed
sections.b: Luke's temple scene is brief: Jesus drives out the sellers, quotes Isaiah 56:7 (without "for all the nations") and Jeremiah 7:11, and then teaches in the temple every day (Luke 19:45–48; 21:37–38). All his last public debates happen there (Luke 20). When some admire its beautiful stones and dedicated gifts, he says not one stone will be left on another (Luke 21:5–6), fulfilled when the Romans burned and leveled it in AD 70. Yet Luke's Gospel ends with the disciples praising God in the temple (Luke 24:53), and the first believers kept meeting there (Acts 2:46).
sections.refs: Luke 19:45–48; Luke 21:5–6; Luke 21:37–38; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Luke 24:53; Acts 2:46

sections.h: Luke: tribute to Caesar and the charge at the trial
sections.b: Luke's form of the question uses phoros, the tribute a subject people paid Rome (the word of Romans 13:6–7), and says the questioners meant to hand Jesus "over to the governor's rule and authority" (Luke 20:20–26). His answer, "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God," is the same as in Matthew and Mark. Only Luke then reports that the leaders accused Jesus before Pilate: "He hinders people from paying taxes to Caesar" (Luke 23:2), a charge his readers know is false; Pilate three times finds him innocent. Luke-Acts repeatedly shows Rome's officials judging the Christians harmless.

sections.h: Luke 20: children of the resurrection
sections.b: Luke's answer to the Sadducees adds to Mark's: "The children of this age take wives and are given as wives. But those who are found worthy to reach that age and the resurrection from the dead neither take wives nor are given as wives. For they can never die again. They are the equals of angels, and they are children of God, being children of the resurrection" (Luke 20:34–36). He also adds "for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38), close to 4 Maccabees 7:19, where the patriarchs "live to God." Luke contrasts two ages, this one, where people marry because they die, and the age to come, where they no longer die.
sections.refs: Luke 20:27–40; Exodus 3:6; 4 Maccabees 7:19; Daniel 12:2–3; Acts 24:15; Mark 12:18–27

common: Jesus does not deny that the risen have bodies (Luke 24:39), only that they marry or die.

sections.h: Luke: the Sadducees' only appearance in the Gospel
sections.b: The Sadducees appear in Luke's Gospel only once, with their riddle of the woman married to seven brothers (Luke 20:27–40), and Luke introduces them as "the ones who deny there is any resurrection." Jesus answers from the Torah, which they accepted, with God's words at the bush. In Acts they become the apostles' chief opponents, "annoyed that they were teaching the people and announcing in Jesus the resurrection from the dead" (Acts 4:1–2; 5:17), and Paul divides the council by appealing to the resurrection against them (Acts 23:6–8).

sections.h: Luke's version: in the temple, with Jerusalem's siege
sections.b: Luke sets the discourse in the temple courts, not on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:5–36), and the disciples ask only about the temple's fall. He adds warnings against those who say "the time has drawn near" and that the end will "not come right away" (Luke 21:8–9); places persecution before the signs (Luke 21:12); replaces Mark's "abomination of desolation" with "Jerusalem being encircled by army camps" (Luke 21:20); adds captivity and "the times of the Gentiles" (Luke 21:24); and ends with a call to sobriety and prayer, "to take your stand before the Son of Man" (Luke 21:34–36). Luke's version thus separates the fall of Jerusalem from the coming of the Son of Man more clearly than Mark's or Matthew's.

common: Most scholars think Luke rewrote Mark 13 in the light of AD 70.
uncommon: Some argue that Luke's siege language comes from the Old Testament and that Luke wrote before 70.

sections.h: "Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled"
sections.b: Only Luke has this phrase: "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). The "until" has been read as setting a limit to Jerusalem's judgment, after which the city or the Jewish people will be restored (dispensational and many evangelical readings, often linked with Romans 11:25); as the age of the Gentile mission, after which "all Israel will be saved" within the church (many Reformed and Catholic readings); or simply as the time between AD 70 and Christ's return. See the card on Luke 21.

sections.h: Luke: the Son of Man in a cloud
sections.b: Luke describes the coming of the Son of Man "in a cloud, with power and much glory" (Luke 21:27), using the singular that links it to the ascension, where "a cloud received him" (Acts 1:9) and the angels promise he "will come this same way, just as you watched him go into the sky" (Acts 1:11). His followers are to "stand tall and raise your heads, for your redemption is getting close" (Luke 21:28). Luke also warns against those who say "the time has drawn near" (Luke 21:8) and asks whether the Son of Man will find faith on the earth (Luke 18:8).

sections.h: Luke 18–21: Luke's own touches
sections.b: In these chapters Luke's distinct voice shows in the two prayer parables (Luke 18:1–14), the Zacchaeus story with its "today" and "son of Abraham" (Luke 19:1–10), the minas parable framed by a claimant to a throne (Luke 19:11–27), the King and the peace in the disciples' song (Luke 19:38), Jesus' tears over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44), and a discourse that separates Jerusalem's fall from the end (Luke 21:20–28). His needle (belonē, Luke 18:25) was once cited as a doctor's word, a claim Henry Cadbury refuted. Luke rejoins Mark's order at Luke 18:15 after his long journey section.

sections.h: Luke 18: what following costs, and what it gives
sections.b: The rich leader is asked to sell everything and follow (Luke 18:22); Peter says, "We left what was ours and followed you," and Jesus promises that no one who has left home, wife, brothers, parents or children for the kingdom will fail to get back many times as much now and eternal life in the age to come (Luke 18:28–30). Luke alone lists a wife among the things left. The healed blind man "began following Jesus" on the road to Jerusalem (Luke 18:43), a picture of the disciple who sees.

sections.h: Archelaus and the parable of the minas
sections.b: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus sailed to Rome to have the kingship confirmed by Augustus; a delegation of fifty Jews followed to oppose him, and he returned as ethnarch of Judea, having already killed about three thousand people at a Passover riot (Josephus, Antiquities 17.299–314; War 2.10–13, 80–92). Jesus' parable of the nobleman who "set out for a distant land, to have the kingship given to him," whose citizens sent envoys saying, "We do not want this man to rule as king over us," and who slaughtered his enemies on his return (Luke 19:12, 14, 27), would have reminded his hearers of this. Luke places it at Jericho, where Archelaus had rebuilt the palace.

sections.h: Luke 19 and 21: grief, not rejection
sections.b: Jesus' words over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44) and on its siege, "wrath on this people" (Luke 21:23), were often read from the second century on as God's final rejection of the Jews, which fed centuries of contempt. Luke's text does not draw that conclusion: Jesus weeps over the city, the judgment is limited "until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24), and in Acts thousands of Jews in Jerusalem believe (Acts 2:41; 21:20). The parable of the tenants is told so that the leaders "could tell he had aimed this parable at them" (Luke 20:19), while the people side with Jesus.

sections.h: Luke 21:20: armies in place of the abomination
sections.b: Where Mark has "when you see 'the abomination of desolation' standing where he must not stand" (Mark 13:14) and Matthew adds "in a holy place" (Matthew 24:15), Luke has "when you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). Luke keeps the word "desolation" (erēmōsis) from Daniel's phrase but turns it into the city's ruin. Many read this as Luke's interpretation of Mark after AD 70; others as a different form of Jesus' warning, based on the prophets' siege language.
